---
title: "Assignment B — Gradient methods for dose-response curves"
subtitle: "Numerical accuracy, momentum, learning rates and local conditioning"
---

# Scope and setup

We compare full-gradient and single-observation gradient methods for nonlinear
least squares. The main question is when momentum or adaptive scaling helps,
and how that depends on starting values, step sizes, local geometry and N.
Newton is excluded from the method comparison. An independent multi-start BFGS
calculation supplies a numerical reference; it is not a competing timed method.

Open `assignment_4.Rproj` and render this document. All settings and experiment
runners are in `project_B/experiments.R`. The [performance report](dose_response_performance.html)
uses the same main cases and geometry experiments. Timings are measured afresh;
seeded data and optimization paths are reproducible, wall times are not identical.
Source only project B's helpers in the R session.

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source("project_B/model.R")
source("project_B/data.R")
source("project_B/solvers.R")
source("project_B/experiments.R")
source("project_B/plots.R")
library(ggplot2)
settings <- study_settings()
settings$batch_size <- 16
cases <- study_data(settings)
grid_data <- cases[["grid_300"]]
problem <- grid_data$problem
```

# Model and simulated data

For $z=\log(x)$, let $q=\operatorname{logistic}(\alpha-\beta z)$ and
$$f(x;\theta)=\gamma+(\delta-\gamma)q,\qquad
Y_i=f(x_i;\theta_{\mathrm{true}})+\varepsilon_i,\quad
\varepsilon_i\sim N(0,0.1^2).$$
We minimize the **mean** squared error,
$$H(\theta)=\frac1N\sum_i(f_i-y_i)^2.$$

| Main design | Log-doses | True $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta)$ | Common start |
|---|---|---|---|
| Grid | Balanced repetitions of $1,\ldots,15$ | $(8,1,0.2,1.2)$ | $(6,0.8,0.1,1.3)$ |
| Continuous | Independent $N(0,2^2)$ values | $(0,1.2,0.2,1.2)$ | $(-0.5,0.8,0.1,1.3)$ |

For each design, generate N = 15,000 once with seed 2026, then use the first 300
observations for the smaller sample. All methods receive the same data and start
within a case. Grid points are repeated deterministically; response noise is random.
Continuous doses are almost surely distinct. The designs also have different true
parameters, so comparing them does not isolate dose placement alone.

The plateau parameters are gamma and delta; `gamma0` denotes a learning rate.
The midpoint of the curve is at $z=\alpha/\beta$. The symmetry
$(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta)\mapsto(-\alpha,-\beta,\delta,\gamma)$ leaves the curve
unchanged, so compare objectives and curves before interpreting parameter differences.

# Gradient and geometry

Let $D=\delta-\gamma$, $w_i=q_i(1-q_i)$ and $r_i=f_i-y_i$. Then
$$J_i=\nabla f_i=(Dw_i,-Dz_iw_i,1-q_i,q_i)^T,$$
$$\nabla H=\frac2N\sum_i r_iJ_i,\qquad
\nabla^2H=\frac2N\sum_i[J_iJ_i^T+r_i\nabla^2f_i].$$
The residual term can make the Hessian indefinite. This objective is generally
nonconvex: small gradients establish approximate stationarity, not a global optimum.
The Hessian remains in the project for derivative tests and geometry diagnostics;
none of the compared methods uses it for an update.

# Methods and step-size rules

| Label | Gradient information | Step rule |
|---|---|---|
| Full GD: Armijo | All N observations | Armijo backtracking |
| Full Polyak: Armijo | All N observations, gradient averaging | Armijo with restart safeguard |
| Full Nesterov: Armijo | All N observations at a look-ahead point | Armijo with restart safeguard |
| Full GD: decay | One batch containing all N observations | Power-law schedule |
| SGD | One observation per update | Power-law schedule |
| Stochastic Polyak | One observation, gradient averaging | Power-law schedule |
| Stochastic Nesterov | One observation at a look-ahead point | Power-law schedule |
| AdaGrad | One observation per update | Fixed base rate, coordinate adaptation |

Ordinary deterministic GD is already a full-batch method. The additional **Full GD:
decay** control separates the scheduled full-gradient implementation from Armijo GD.
It makes only one update per epoch, whereas SGD makes N. Thus their equal-pass
comparison changes both gradient noise and the number of updates; it is not a pure
experiment on noise alone.

For stochastic algorithms, each epoch randomly permutes the observations and visits
each once. Batch size is one. Momentum state persists between epochs. With
$g_t$ denoting the appropriate full or individual gradient, Polyak uses the course's
averaging convention:
$$\rho_t=m\rho_{t-1}+(1-m)g_t,\qquad
\theta_t=\theta_{t-1}-\eta_t\rho_t,\quad \rho_0=0.$$
Nesterov first extrapolates:
$$u_t=\theta_{t-1}+m(\theta_{t-1}-\theta_{t-2}),\qquad
\theta_t=u_t-\eta_t g_t(u_t).$$
We use $m=0.9$, with the first displacement zero. These are not claims of the
optimal convex accelerated rate for this nonconvex stochastic problem.

For the scheduled methods, completed epochs $e=0,1,\ldots$ determine
$$\eta_e=\frac{\eta_0K}{K+e^{0.75}},\qquad K=5^{0.75}.$$
The initial rate is 0.01 and halves after five completed epochs. It remains constant
within an epoch. AdaGrad instead keeps its base rate at 0.01 and updates elementwise:
$$s_t=s_{t-1}+g_t^2,\qquad
\theta_t=\theta_{t-1}-0.01\,\frac{g_t}{\sqrt{s_t+10^{-8}}}.$$
Its effective coordinate rates decrease without another decay schedule.

## Armijo and deterministic momentum safeguards

Given a base point $b$ and descent direction $d$, halve the trial step from 1 until
$$H(b+\eta d)\le H(b)+10^{-4}\eta\nabla H(b)^Td.$$
The trial step resets on every iteration. All three full-gradient Armijo methods
share this rule, a 2,000-update budget and gradient infinity-norm tolerance $10^{-8}$.

For GD and Polyak the base point is the current iterate. If Polyak's averaged
gradient points uphill, reset its memory before searching. For Nesterov, apply
Armijo at the look-ahead point, then additionally require that the result does not
increase the objective relative to the current iterate. If it does, discard the
extrapolation and take an Armijo GD step; reset the next displacement to zero.
A failed momentum search also retries as GD. Failure of that search is reported.

These are explicitly **safeguarded momentum variants**, rather than the unmodified
fixed-step course algorithms. Restarts are reported: frequent restarts indicate
that the momentum proposal was often unhelpful. Sharing controls makes comparisons
transparent, but does not make methods equally tuned or their per-update costs equal.

# Correctness checks

```{r}
#| label: tests
testthat::test_dir("tests/project_B", reporter = "summary", stop_on_failure = TRUE)
```

The readable tests check numerical derivatives, exact grouping, individual-gradient
averaging, the course's SGD loop, agreement with independent nonlinear least squares,
non-increasing accepted deterministic losses, the first momentum updates without
restarts, full-batch gradient scaling, and equality of R/C++ gradients. These tests
check implementations; they do not prove global convergence.

# Two-dimensional trajectories

Fix gamma and delta at their true grid values and vary alpha and beta, from the same
two starts for every method. The star is a conditional multi-start BFGS reference.
Circles mark starts, triangles last recorded points. These are 15-epoch stochastic
runs and at most 2,000 Armijo updates. Paths connect recorded iterates, not time.
The rate shown applies to scheduled methods and AdaGrad; Armijo trial steps stay at 1.

```{r}
#| label: slice
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-height: 11
plot_slice(problem, fixed = grid_data$truth,
           starts = rbind(c(6, 0.6), c(10, 1.4)), gamma0 = 0.05)
```

```{r}
#| label: slice-larger-rate
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-height: 11
plot_slice(problem, fixed = grid_data$truth,
           starts = rbind(c(6, 0.6), c(10, 1.4)), gamma0 = 0.1)
```

The third dimension is log10(MSE). It reveals small loss differences but changes
apparent curvature: it cannot be used to read off a condition number. Blue and orange
identify the two starts. Trajectories are drawn over the surface for visibility.

```{r}
#| label: slice-surface
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-height: 11
plot_slice(problem, grid_data$truth, rbind(c(6, 0.6), c(10, 1.4)),
           gamma0 = 0.05, view = "surface")
```

```{r}
#| label: slice-surface-larger-rate
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-height: 11
plot_slice(problem, grid_data$truth, rbind(c(6, 0.6), c(10, 1.4)),
           gamma0 = 0.1, view = "surface")
```

Look for progress across versus along the valley. Alpha and beta can partly compensate
through their ratio. Stochastic updates need not reduce the full MSE; momentum can
help sustained movement but also overshoot. The full-gradient variants illustrate
how much of the oscillation depends on sampling and how much the safeguards remove.

# Main comparison: small and large N

Every stochastic run gets 15 epochs, using shuffle seeds 201 and 202. These vary
optimization order, not the simulated dataset. Full GD with decay is run once;
reshuffling a full batch changes only floating-point summation. Full MSE monitoring
occurs every quarter epoch where possible and is included in elapsed time. Full-batch
scheduled GD can only record once per epoch because there is only one update.

Report the final MSE, status and first recorded time within $10^{-4}$ of the
best-found reference. NA means no recorded attainment within budget, not missing
failure data. First attainment does not imply remaining below the target. Small
negative reference differences remain visible and would warrant a better reference
search. The reference is not a certified global optimum.

```{r}
#| label: main-study
results <- run_study(settings)
comparison <- study_summary(results, settings)
main_rows <- comparison[!startsWith(comparison$run, "grouped_"), ]
knitr::kable(main_rows[, c("design", "N", "method", "seed", "status", "updates", "objective",
                         "seconds", "seconds_to_target", "restarts")],
             digits = 6, row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: main-convergence
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 10
plot_study(results)
```

```{r}
#| label: small-sample-detail
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 6
plot_study(results[c("grid_300", "continuous_300")])
```

Each panel has its own time scale and a shared MSE scale. Compare the numerical
time-axis labels rather than horizontal distances across panels.

Increasing N gives more stochastic updates per epoch, but also more work. Compare
wall time rather than iteration counts. A similar order of MSE is not equal accuracy;
near the noise variance 0.01, the reference differences and target times are useful.
A method stopping at its budget has not necessarily converged. Short timings are
limited by timer resolution; repeated computational benchmarks follow in the other report.

## Fitted and generating curves

```{r}
#| label: fitted-curves
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6
for (name in names(results)) {
  case <- results[[name]]
  selected <- c("full_gd", "full_polyak", "full_nesterov", "full_decay",
                "sgd_201", "polyak_201", "nesterov_201", "adagrad_201")
  print(plot_curves(case$dataset, case$fits[selected]) + ggtitle(name))
}
```

The dashed black line is the generating curve; at most 1,500 observations are plotted,
although every observation is used in fitting. Display seed 201 for stochastic curves;
both seeds remain in the convergence comparison.

# One factor at a time: starting values

Keep N = 300, the grid data and all controls fixed. Use a near-truth start
$(7.5,0.9,0.15,1.25)$, the baseline $(6,0.8,0.1,1.3)$ and a saturated start
$(20, 2, 0.5, 2.3)$. These intentionally probe favorable and difficult initializations;
the near-truth case uses knowledge available only in simulation. Compare all methods,
including runs that fail to reach the reference.

```{r}
#| label: start-sensitivity
#| results: asis
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6
start_results <- run_sensitivity(settings, "starts")
for (name in names(start_results)) {
  case <- start_results[[name]]
  print(knitr::kable(fit_summary(case$fits, case$dataset$problem, case$reference),
                     digits = 6, row.names = FALSE, caption = name))
  print(plot_convergence(case$fits, case$reference) + ggtitle(name))
}
```

# One factor at a time: step sizes

First vary only the scheduled/AdaGrad initial rate: 0.001, 0.01, 0.05. Keep starts,
data, seeds, momentum and decay half-time fixed. AdaGrad still uses a fixed base rate.
Then vary only the Armijo trial step: 0.1, 1, 5, keeping c fixed. Armijo can shorten
an excessive trial step, at the cost of extra objective evaluations. These are
separate experiments because a trial step and a scheduled rate play different roles.

```{r}
#| label: rate-sensitivity
#| results: asis
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6
for (experiment in c("stochastic_rate", "armijo_step")) {
  rate_results <- run_sensitivity(settings, experiment)
  for (name in names(rate_results)) {
    case <- rate_results[[name]]
    print(knitr::kable(fit_summary(case$fits, case$dataset$problem, case$reference),
                       digits = 6, row.names = FALSE, caption = name))
    print(plot_convergence(case$fits, case$reference) + ggtitle(name))
  }
}
```

# One factor at a time: underlying slope and local conditioning

Use 1,500 identical continuous log-doses and the same noise realization for all three
cases. Keep alpha = 0, gamma = 0.2 and delta = 1.2, but set the true beta to
0.35, 1.2 or 4. A shallow sigmoid can appear almost linear over the sampled range;
a steep sigmoid concentrates information near its transition. Both can weaken
identification in some directions. We measure rather than presume the outcome.

All methods use the same continuous-design start and controls. Changing the true
slope also changes the start's distance to the solution, so this is a geometry
stress test, not a perfectly isolated experiment on a single condition number.

The table shows exact Hessian eigenvalues and, when positive definite, their ratio.
It also shows the eigenvalue ratio of $2J^TWJ$, with $W=I/N$, a positive-semidefinite
local curvature diagnostic. At the generating parameters this is the conditional
expected Hessian over response noise. Neither number is a global $L/\mu$ bound.
Condition numbers depend on parameter units; units are unchanged across these cases.
NA indicates an exact Hessian that is not positive definite; Inf indicates numerical
singularity under the diagnostic threshold.

```{r}
#| label: geometry
#| results: asis
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6
geometry_results <- run_sensitivity(settings, "geometry")
knitr::kable(geometry_summary(geometry_results), digits = 4, row.names = FALSE)
for (name in names(geometry_results)) {
  case <- geometry_results[[name]]
  print(knitr::kable(fit_summary(case$fits, case$dataset$problem, case$reference),
                     digits = 6, row.names = FALSE, caption = name))
  print(plot_convergence(case$fits, case$reference) + ggtitle(name))
  selected <- c("full_gd", "full_polyak", "full_nesterov", "full_decay",
                "sgd_201", "polyak_201", "nesterov_201", "adagrad_201")
  print(plot_curves(case$dataset, case$fits[selected]) + ggtitle(name))
}
```

For this seed, the exact Hessian condition numbers at the numerical references
are approximately 493, 103 and 970 for slopes 0.35, 1.2 and 4, respectively.
The middle slope is locally better conditioned in these parameter units. This
supports the intended geometry contrast without asserting a global ordering of
optimization difficulty.

Relate slow loss reduction to local geometry, then inspect whether momentum helps
and whether it triggers restarts or oscillations. AdaGrad scales coordinates using
gradient history, not the Hessian; it need not correct a rotated narrow valley.
Do not select a favorable run as proof that a method is generally superior.

# Link to computation

The performance report uses the same sample-size and geometry experiments. It
compares achieved accuracy with elapsed time, explains costs of full versus individual
gradients, measures line-search work, and benchmarks exact grid compression. Grouping
changes evaluation cost without changing the objective. Profiling and Rcpp then
identify potential implementation improvements. Mini-batches remain an extension;
the main stochastic comparisons use one observation per update.
